Items.Authors: Joaquin Garcia
Items.Title: Operational Science as a Catalyst for Innovation: Knowledge Transfer from Observatory Environments to Machine Learning Research
Items.Abstract: Scientific observatories are not only centers of data collection but also places that encourage innovation and learning. This contribution shows how daily exposure to interferometric concepts at ALMA, such as correlation, signal coherence, and noise robustness, can inspire new ideas in machine learning. As a case study, we present RefractedSpeech, a project that adapts methods from interferometric data processing to create acoustic descriptors based on autocorrelation and cross-correlation analysis. These features improved robustness to environmental noise and allowed clearer model interpretation through tools such as SHAP. The work highlights how the operational environment at ALMA can stimulate creative problem-solving among engineering and computing staff and supports the idea that knowledge transfer between operational science and other research fields can strengthen both technical and scientific capabilities.

Items.Authors: Ivan Lloro, John Hawke, André van Es, Caroline Jaillot, Robert Haigh, Mark Waterson, Antony Schinckel, Jimi Green, George Heald, Lucio Tirone, Peter Dewdney, Robert Laing
Items.Title: SKA-Low status update
Items.Abstract: The Square Kilometre Array–Low (SKA-Low) telescope is entering a decisive construction phase. Civil and electrical infrastructure at Inyarrimanha Ilgari Bundara, CSIRO's Murchison Radio-astronomy Observatory, is nearing completion, enabling large-scale station deployment and installation of power, networking, and timing systems. Station roll-out is accelerating, with prototype and early-production elements undergoing validation against performance, calibration, electromagnetic compatibility, and environmental criteria. Key milestones have been achieved in correlator-beamformer commissioning, while parallel progress in the software ecosystem enables increasingly realistic end-to-end testing. Data-flow orchestration, calibration pipelines, and quality-assurance mechanisms are being refined for early operations. This paper outlines achieved milestones, remaining technical risks, and the trajectory toward commissioning of the first operational SKA-Low stations to enable science capability.

Items.Authors: Titouan Le Goff, Clément Lobre, Olivier Gravrand, Bertrand Hoarau, Amaury Mavel, Jocelyn Berthoz, Céline Riuné, Florent Rochette
Items.Title: Technology advancements in Very Long-Wave Infrared (VLWIR) Imagers for Future European Space Missions
Items.Abstract: Future European space missions demand high-performance very long-wave infrared (VLWIR) imagers with >15 µm cutoff, operating at 65K in TV-format arrays (15 µm pitch). This work presents the first realization of photodiodes in this spectral range and focal plane arrays (FPAs) addressing critical challenges of narrow-bandgap materials.   Tests arrays with P on N new generation technology under development at CEA and Lynred were manufactured and evaluated at higher temperature (80K). The aim of this first batch was to address first order figures of merit and a solution for debiasing, a key limitation in VLWIR range. The results demonstrate successful mitigation of debiasing without compromising operability >99.5% at 80K, reverse plateaus >100 mV, and dark currents in the expected range.  Further refinement of the technology will rely on advanced characterization performed by our partner IFAE, targeting quantum efficiency optimization and noise issues such as low-temperature dark current.

Items.Authors: Youwei Yao, Raul Riveros, Joseph Colosimo, Jessica Patel, Kai-wing Chan, Takashi Okajima, William Zhang, Kristin Madsen
Items.Title: Development of zero net-stress coatings for future X-ray missions
Items.Abstract: We report recent progress of developing zero net-stress x-ray coatings at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC). Future x-ray telescope missions such as AXIS require reflective coatings on extremely thin mirror shells to achieve both high throughput and sub-arcsecond angular resolution. As the heritage of missions including Chandra and NuSTAR, the DC magnetron sputtering method can deliver high-quality and stable x-ray coatings. However, the intrinsic compressive stress can induce significant distortions on thin mirrors, therefore degrading angular resolution. Our group at GSFC has developed a UV-based direct printing method to pattern silicon oxide layers on the backside of the mirrors for precise stress compensation. This approach is precise, low cost and ready for mass production. Results including interferometry and x-ray testing demonstrate feasible precision and satisfied repeatability, making this technique promising for future x-ray telescope missions.

Items.Authors: Richard Davies, Joao Alves, Yann Clénet, Florian Lang, Seppo Mattila, Anna Monna, Jörg-Uwe Pott, Sebastian Rabien, Sebastian Schaeffer, Mario Schweitzer, Eckhard Sturm, Eline Tolstoy, Benedetta Vulcani
Items.Title: The MICADO first light imager for the ELT: from cold integration towards science operations
Items.Abstract: MICADO is now well into its assembly, integration, and test phase; and is on track for first light of the ELT at the end of the decade. This contribution will provide an overview of the instrument and its main sub-systems, describing the status of each of them, the milestones that have been achieved, and the progress in the current cold integration phase towards achieving first light through the fully assembled cryostat from the entrance window to the focal plane array. It will also provide a glimpse of how it might look to operate MICADO and prepare observations. It will finish with an outlook towards the next steps leading up to commissioning of the instrument at the ELT.

Items.Authors: Peter S. Barry
Items.Title: An Overview and Future Plans for the Shirokoff Line Intensity Mapper on the South Pole Telescope
Items.Abstract: The Shirokoff Line Intensity Mapper (SLIM) is a millimeter-wave line-intensity mapping experiment developed for the South Pole Telescope (SPT). SPT-SLIM serves as both a technical and scientific pathfinder, demonstrating the feasibility and in-field performance of multi-pixel superconducting filterbank spectrometers for future mm-LIM surveys.    SPT-SLIM was commissioned at the SPT during the 2024–2025 austral summer. The focal plane comprises nine dual-polarization pixels coupled to an ortho-mode transducer, with each polarization fed to an R = 100 thin-film microstrip filterbank covering the 2 mm window (120–180 GHz). We present an overview of the instrument, including detector design and characterization, highlights from commissioning, and principal on-sky results from the Year 1 deployment. We also report on ongoing upgrades and performance of the enhanced focal plane in preparation for the upcoming Year 2 season.

Items.Authors: Mason Black, Deborah F. Woods, Louis Perna
Items.Title: Efficient detection of faint geostationary and cislunar objects in Rubin LSST imagery
Items.Abstract: The Vera C. Rubin Observatory’s exceptional sensitivity could make it a powerful tool for cataloging and tracking very faint objects in geostationary or cislunar orbits. However, the ~30 s exposure time can cause streaks from such objects to span thousands of pixels across the CCDs. This fast apparent motion results in per-pixel fluxes well below the detectability threshold for point sources. Objects that would be easily detectable if they had no apparent motion are dwarfed by the per-pixel sky noise, limiting the effectiveness of conventional streak detection. We present an efficient real-time streak detection approach that is able to recover detection sensitivities approaching the theoretical limit. This method is demonstrated using LSST Commissioning Camera images applied to the detection of synthetic streaks injected into real images.

Items.Authors: Yoshinori Suematsu, Naoki Kohara, Toshihiro Tsuzuki, Hideki Takami
Items.Title: Evaluation of stitching error in interferometric stitching measurements of large-aperture telescope
Items.Abstract: High-precision optical testing of large-aperture telescopes requires accurate wavefront-error evaluation using interferometric stitching. To obtain reliable full-aperture wavefront measurements, it is essential to understand how subaperture measurement errors, caused by environmental disturbances and interferometer misalignment, propagate into the stitched result. This study evaluates the influence of these subaperture errors on overall stitching accuracy and defines achievable tolerances for subaperture-interferometer performance. We developed a numerical stitching method that compensates for random wavefront errors introduced by misalignments and environmental effects. Simulations under multiple random-error conditions showed that the stitching error was comparable to or smaller than the individual random measurement errors. We present the simulation methodology, the influence of random measurement errors, and the achievable stitching accuracy.

Items.Authors: Nithyanandan Thyagarajan, Samuel Lai, Ivy Wong, Foivos Diakogiannis
Items.Title: Independent event horizon imaging of the supermassive black holes in M87 and the Milky Way
Items.Abstract: The Event Horizon Telescope's images of the supermassive black holes in M87 and the Milky Way required pushing VLBI imaging to its limits, underscoring the importance of independent analyses. We present a fully independent approach comprising an independent team, independent reconstruction methodology based entirely on independent observables (closure invariants), which are immune to calibration errors. Using the public EHT datasets, we apply GenDIReCT, a diffusion-based generative imaging framework operating in the latent space of images conditioned on closure invariants. This calibration-independent strategy provides an independent view of the underlying horizon-scale structure and offers a complementary pathway for interpreting the data under extreme observational conditions. We show results for both M87 and Milky Way black holes, demonstrating the potential of closure-driven, AI-enabled imaging as a powerful new direction for VLBI studies at the highest angular resolutions.

Items.Authors: Kaila Hall-Smith
Items.Title: Managing interfaces for the SKAO telescopes
Items.Abstract: Managing the significantly large number of interfaces within both the SKAO Telescopes is a challenging task. The global nature of this project means ensuring the interface model represents the source of truth has been a involved problem. Until now the status and ownership of these interfaces has been buried in technical documents and information regarding the interfaces spread across different platforms. Using Cameo Enterprise Architecture and various other tools we have developed a process to not only display the vast number of interfaces in a simple intuitive way but to present the live status of the ICDs that define them in dashboards that allow easy tracking through the lifecycle of the system. This view of the system has dramatically improved our understanding of the areas of the system that need attention and allowed us to drive the progress. This paper will present the steps of this process, the tools used and how the different types of information are presented and distributed.

Items.Authors: Christopher A. Haniff, Juan Paulo Barios, David F. Buscher, Martin Fisher, Eugene B. Seneta, John S. Young, Van D. Romero, Michelle J. Creech-Eakman, Caelan F. Eakman, Emma Floyd, Anders M. Jorgensen, James Luis, Jeffrey C. Mason, Andres Olivares, Sam Rochelle, Chris Salcido, Raphael Santoro, Ian S. Schofield
Items.Title: Validating the capability of the Magdalena Ridge Observatory Interferometer (MROI) for GEO satellite imaging
Items.Abstract: A goal of the Magdalena Ridge Observatory Interferometer (MROI) is to enable model-independent imaging of faint targets. This addresses a key problem for satellites in geosynchronous (GEO) and medium Earth orbit (MEO) where imaging modalities struggle to deliver the milliarcsecond resolution and faint-source capability required. We report on initial MROI observations of a sample of GEO targets aimed at realising an imaging capability with a sparse ground-based optical array and confirm the sustained detection of interferometric fringes from the communications satellite Eutelsat West 115B. Our focus has been on validating the performance of the most critical optomechanical subsystems of the MROI required for GEO imaging, on the management of observations of non-sidereal objects, and on the operability of the array for studies of resolved GEO satellites. The impact of these data on the development of the MROI and the capability of spatial interferometry for GEO asset SSA is discussed.

Items.Authors: Michael F. Sterzik, J. Brinchmann, J. Grave, U. Grothkopf, O. Hainaut, A. Kaufer, T. Klein, S. Meakins, A. Mérand, S. Mieske, F. Patat, C. Peroux, M. Rejkuba, M. Romaniello, M Hilker
Items.Title: 25 years of impact: science return of the Very Large Telescope
Items.Abstract: The scientific performance of an observatory depends on how observing programs are implemented and executed. After more than 25 years of continuous and stable operations of the VLT, the Paranal Observatory provides a uniquely rich dataset to quantify the long-term effects of the implementations of science policy strategies on scientific return.  We use bibliometric indicators to evaluate program productivity and to characterize how different program types (Normal, Large, Guaranteed Time Observations, Director Discretionary Time, Target of Opportunity) and observing modes (aka Visitor and Service) translate into scientific publications.   The long operational baseline of the VLT enables us to identify trends in scientific return, its connection to evolving operational strategies, and the contribution of specific program classes to high-impact publications. In particular, we highlight the increasing contributions of ESO's science archive to the publication statistics.

Items.Authors: Robyn J. Sharman
Items.Title: Evaluating linear-mode avalanche photodiode arrays for Gaia NIR.
Items.Abstract: Gaia NIR is a proposed follow on to the highly successful Gaia mission. While Gaia made use of CCD devices to perform on-chip time-delay integration (TDI), Gaia NIR will require off-chip TDI with frames read out continuously during rotation. The coaddition of these frames will give a TDI-like performance, but only where read noise is effectively zero. The UK ATC is working with Leonardo UK, the University of Cambridge, and MSSL on a de-risking activity for the Gaia NIR mission, which aims to demonstrate the feasibility of using LmAPD arrays to achieve this performance. As part of this de-risking activity, Leonardo UK have provided the UK ATC with three HgCdTe LmAPD arrays for characterisation and evaluation at high gain. The arrays are each bonded to a 320x256 pixel SAPHIRA ROIC with a 24um pixel pitch. This paper will discuss the development of the UK ATC photon-counting test facility as well as the preliminary results from our investigations of the Leonardo UK LmAPD arrays.

Items.Authors: Jooyun Woo, Yue Yu, Jaime R. Armendariz, Desiree D. M. Ferreira, Peter L. Henriksen, Eftychia Kotsiou, Sonny Massahi, Kerstin Perez, Anacorina Romero, Vyshnavi Sabbi, Marcela Stern, Julia K. Vogel, Ipek Altunyurt
Items.Title: Fabrication and expected performance of the inner-core X-ray optic for BabyIAXO
Items.Abstract: BabyIAXO, a prototype for the International Axion Observatory (IAXO), is the first axion helioscope to employ X-ray optics matched to the magnetic bore. The optic consists of a thermally formed inner core and a cold-slumped outer corona, both constructed from segmented glass substrates. To fabricate the inner-core optic, we systematized the thermal-forming procedure, leveraging techniques developed for NuSTAR. The quality of free-standing glass substrates was characterized by laser metrology, X-ray reflectometry, and atomic force microscopy. We developed a cutting technique that produces smooth edges at the micron scale. We used flat stacks of glass-epoxy-graphite layers to evaluate the performance of the epoxy bondline. We present the expected performance of the assembled inner-core optic.

Items.Authors: Sandrine J. Thomas, Andrew Connolly, John Franklin Crenshaw, Bryce Kalmbach, Petr Kubanek, Guillem Megias, Josh Meyer, Bekah Polen, Bruno Quint, Aaron Roodman, Chris Suberlak, Elana Urbach
Items.Title: Rubin optical system integration and commissioning
Items.Abstract: The Vera C. Rubin Observatory’s Simonyi Survey Telescope, an 8.4m telescope in Chile, will soon begin a decade-long optical sky survey, the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST). To achieve exceptional image quality across its 3.5° field of view, the telescope uses a unique three-mirror design, advanced optics, and a robust active optics system (AOS) to maintain alignment and mirror shape. This paper covers the final integration and commissioning of the telescope’s optics, highlighting recent integration steps and optical coating performance. The focus is on the AOS and its effectiveness. Additionally, precise thermal control of the combined primary and tertiary (M1M3) borosilicate mirror and telescope top-end is essential, as some thermal effects cannot be corrected by the AOS alone. These systems ensure consistent, high-quality observations throughout the survey.

Items.Authors: Dirk Schmidt, Nicolas Gorceix, Vasyl Yurchyshyn, Thomas R. Rimmele, Philip R. Goode, Thomas A. Schad
Items.Title: What is that? Observing in the Sun's corona at 10x increased resolution enabled by adaptive optics
Items.Abstract: You will see spectacular videos in this presentation of highly-dynamic small-scale features in the Sun’s corona - its atmosphere - such as prominences and coronal rain revealed by the use of adaptive optics (AO). Cona - the first coronal AO system - is installed at the1.6-meter Goode Solar Telescope and is optimized for scientific observations of relatively cool and dim plasma features. They peak in the H-alpha line where Cona reaches the diffraction limited of 63 km - an order of magnitude finer than the seeing limit. The Shack-Hartmann sensor works at 2 kHz at intensities similar to laser guide stars. You will see that AO was vital to discover a fascinatingly complex unknown event, which still lacks a plausible physical explanation. Cona has been commissioned for science in 2025. It enables a new class of observations, paving the way for new discoveries. We will show an early concept for coronal AO at the 4-meter Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope (DKIST) for an even finer resolution.

Items.Authors: Adyn Miles, Peter Bartosik, Lun (Steven) Li, Antoine Letarte, Normand Fullum, L. Javier Romualdez, John W. Hartley, Jason VazBrown, Pablo Trujillo, Douglas B. George, Thuy Vy Luu, Steven J. Benton, William C. Jones, C. Barth Netterfield
Items.Title: GigaBIT: design and analysis of a diffraction-limited balloon-borne telescope
Items.Abstract: This paper presents the design of the Gigapixel Balloon-borne Imaging Telescope (GigaBIT), a diffraction-limited, wide-field telescope being developed for a stratospheric test flight in 2027. The GigaBIT design addresses a combination of challenges unique to balloon-borne astronomy, including harsh thermal environments, significant gravity-induced deformations, and disturbances from winds at float altitude. We describe the optical, thermomechanical, and alignment strategies required to meet diffraction-limited performance on a balloon-borne platform, including optical tolerancing, mechanical optimization of a lightweighted mirror, tunable thermal management, and a multi-stage alignment strategy. We also highlight design strategies specific to balloon platforms to inform future balloon-borne astronomy missions.

Items.Authors: Bernhard R. Brandl, Olivier Absil, António Amorim, Ioannis Argyriou, Jean-Christophe Barrière, Thomas Bertram, Felix Bettonvil, Peter Bizenberger, Emilie Bouzerand, Wolfgang Brandner, Gaël Chauvin, Richard Chou, Yigit Dallilar, Dennis Dolkens, Reinhold J. Dorn, Mercedes Filho, Markus Feldt, Paulo Garcia, Juan-Pablo Garcia, Alistair Glasse, Adrian M. Glauser, Manuel Güdel, Christoph Haupt, Ted Huang, Sander Kwast, Lucas Labadie, Kieran Leschinski, Dirk Lesman, Jeff Lynn, Michael Meyer, Gilles Orban de Xivry, Youichi Ohyama, Eric Pantin, Philip Parr-Burman, Ioannis Politopoulos, Sascha Quanz, Gert Raskin, Maddalena Reggiani, Chad Salo, Silvia Scheithauer, Benoît Serra, Ralf Siebenmorgen, Remko Stuik, Niels Tromp, Roy van Boekel, Joost van den Born, Hans Van Winckel, Shiang-Yu Wang
Items.Title: Status of the mid-infrared ELT imager and spectrograph METIS: starting system-level AIT
Items.Abstract: METIS will be one of the first scientific instruments on ESO's 39m Extremely Large Telescope (ELT), providing high contrast imaging and medium resolution slit-spectroscopy, and high resolution (R ~100,000) integral field spectroscopy, all at the ELT's diffraction limit. Manufacturing and testing of optical and opto-mechanical components and subsystems is in full swing. The delivery of the individual subsystems to the new AIT facility at Leiden University has just started. We present early test results, discuss the plans for the upcoming functional and performance test phase, and highlight the challenges in building an ELT instrument.

Items.Authors: Juan Paolo Lorenzo Gerardo Barrios, David F. Buscher, Michelle J. Creech-Eakman, Alireza Esmaeilzadeh, Emma Floyd, Christopher A. Haniff, James Luis, Andres Olivares, Chris Salcido, Rafael Santoro, Ian S. Schofield, Eugene B. Seneta, John S. Young, Daniel J. Ahrer, Ian Baker, Leander Mehrgan
Items.Title: Commissioning FOURIER: the Magdalena Ridge Observatory Interferometer’s first-generation science beam combiner
Items.Abstract: The Magdalena Ridge Observatory Interferometer (MROI) is a 10-telescope optical interferometer under construction in NM, USA as an international collaboration between the New Mexico Institute of Mining and Technology and the University of Cambridge. MROI’s first-generation science beam combiner, FOURIER, measures observables from wavelengths of 1.1 to 2.4 microns using spectrally-dispersed fringes from up to 3 telescopes. In this paper, we report on the results of FOURIER's ongoing commissioning after it was installed at the MROI. We discuss the performance of the instrument's cryostat in terms of vacuum and temperature holding times. We also present the results of detector tests from within the cryostat, including FOURIER's gain curve, photon transfer curves, and system noise. Finally, having achieved our first stellar fringes in July 2025, we present measurements of FOURIER's wavelength calibration, dispersion axis brightness profile, and visibility based on preliminary on-sky tests

Items.Authors: Mark Warner, Christoph Keller, Alexei Pevtsov, Sarah Gajadhar
Items.Title: From blank sheet to global network: practical lessons and best practices standing up the ngGONG design project
Items.Abstract: The ngGONG project will design a next-generation ground-based solar observing network to support long-term heliophysics and space-weather research. This paper describes how the design effort is being stood up “from a blank sheet,” covering early decisions on scope, requirements, governance, staffing, and tools. It highlights practical lessons on creating a project culture, aligning diverse scientific and operational stakeholders, and maintaining momentum in a complex, distributed environment. The focus is on concrete practices and checklists that other large telescope and network design teams can adapt to their own contexts.

Items.Authors: Morteza Pashapour-Ahmadabadi, Dominik J. Schwarz, Aritra Basu, Vincent Eberle, Torsten Ensslin, Philipp Frank, Richard Fuchs, Hans-Rainer Klöckner, Anna Nelles
Items.Title: GAMBIT: a Bayesian framework for radio antenna beam modelling
Items.Abstract: Accurate primary beam models are essential for calibration and imaging in radio astronomy. Traditional approaches either lack flexibility (analytical models) or become computationally expensive for wide-band observations (electromagnetic simulations). We present GAMBIT (Generative Antenna Model from Bayesian Inference Technique), a new framework for primary-beam modelling applied here to holographic MeerKAT L-band data. Built on Information Field Theory (IFT) and implemented in the NIFTy library, GAMBIT represents the beam as a single underlying base pattern subject to three smooth, frequency-dependent geometric transformations per frequency: an isotropic scale factor and two spatial shifts. Inference is performed on holographic Stokes I measurements. The model compresses 67 MB of data per antenna into 150 KB while maintaining reduced Chi-squared ≈1, achieving the lowest mean-squared deviation from the data among parametric, data-driven, and electromagnetic reference models.

Items.Authors: Emile Prêle, Martino Calvo, Usasi Chowdhury, Gregory Garde, Florence Levy-Bertrand, Alessandro Monfardini
Items.Title: On-chip filled array hyperspectral kinetic inductance detectors (FHYKID) for line intensity mapping
Items.Abstract: The next generation Line Intensity Mapping (LIM) experiments will require very high throughput instrumentation, and as a consequence high pixel counts focal planes. For the study of the [CII] line in the redshift range z=7-8, we develop a hyperspectral focal plane (FHYKID) operating in the range 210-240 GHz and with a spectral resolution reaching 120. The spectral filtering is achieved thanks to planar SSRR (Slot Split Ring Resonators) coupled to Lumped Element Kinetic Inductance Detectors (LEKID). This robust concept achieves, thanks to its simplicity, large quantum efficiency and is scalable, even with current readout electronics systems, to several tens of thousands beams on Sky. Our HYPKID will be one of the four channels of the NIKONA instrument, currently seeking funding and to be installed at the 30-meter telescope at Pico Veleta. Among the science goals, simultaneously mapping the local (galactic and nearby-galaxies) CO line and the cosmological [CII].

Items.Authors: Vincent Pollet, Sami Caroff, Pierre Aubert, Thibaut Oprinsen
Items.Title: The real time analysis reconstruction framework of the Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory
Items.Abstract: We will present the current status and recent advances in the real-time analysis (RTA) developed for the Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory (CTAO). Rapidly variable and short-lived gamma-ray phenomena, such as gamma-ray bursts and flaring active galactic nuclei, require low-latency characterization by the RTA to trigger follow-up observations and efficient coordination with other facilities. The first Large Sized Telescope, LST-1, is being used as a test bench and pathfinder for this effort, driving the optimization of real-time algorithms and guiding their integration into the Array Control and Data Acquisition System (ACADA) of CTAO in the Science Alert Generation framework (SAG). In particular, we will discuss the ongoing work to extend the current mono-telescope pipeline towards stereo operation with multiple telescopes, a crucial step to fully exploit the sensitivity and rapid response of the CTAO array for the study of the dynamic universe.

Items.Authors: Danny Gasman, Benoît Serra, Roy van Boekel, Ioannis Argyriou, Daniel Dicken, Vianak Naranjo, Peter Bizenberger
Items.Title: Charge migration characterization in the METIS H2RG detectors
Items.Abstract: The Mid-infrared ELT Imager and Spectrograph (METIS) is one of the first-light instruments of the Extremely Large Telescope (ELT). For the L and M band, the instrument makes use of Teledyne’s H2RG detectors, known to be affected by charge migration, also known as the brighter-fatter effect (BFE). In the H2RG detectors this manifests as photo-electrons moving from a central bright pixel to neighboring pixels as the depletion region of the central pixel decreases with accumulated charge. Due to its effect of ‘blurring’ information, it especially affects direct imaging, transit, and high-resolution spectroscopy applications. Nominal METIS operations will not use up-the-ramp sampling, meaning we cannot cut ramps once the effect becomes too strong. We therefore aim to characterize its effect in the METIS H2RG detectors, such that we can remove it without losing information.

Items.Authors: Hanshin Lee, Herman Kriel, Michael P. Smith, Chris E. Robison, Steven Cadd, Joel L. Larakers
Items.Title: Integration, alignment, and early laboratory performance of the Hobby-Eberly Telescope primary mirror alignment metrology system upgrade
Items.Abstract: The primary mirror (M1) of the Hobby Eberly Telescope (HET) consists of 91 mirror segments in a regular hexagon shape. The M1’s center of curvature can be accessed from the top of a 90ft-tall tower just outside the HET dome. The current alignment metrology system in this tower, called the Center of Curvature Alignment System (CCAS), keeps the 91 segments into a single smooth 11-meter diameter surface. This critical alignment function is at risk due to the obsolescence and deficiencies of the aging system. The upgrade includes a suite of advanced metrology instruments to provide improved alignment precision and metrology. In particular, the upgrade features a new dispersed fringe sensing technique capable of measuring the piston error of all 240 segment edges across M1 in a single-shot exposure. This paper summarizes the final electro-opto-mechanical design of the system and details the integration, alignment, and performance evaluation of the system in Austin laboratories.

Items.Authors: Hannah C. Gulick, Charles-Antoine Claveau, Jessica R. Lu, Kodi Rider, Steven V. Beckwith, Josh Bloom, Wei Liu, Dan Werthimer, Mathew Dexter
Items.Title: CuRIOS-ED: expected on-orbit performance and early flight data from a space-based CMOS imager
Items.Abstract: CuRIOS-ED (CubeSats for Rapid Infrared and Optical Surveys–Exploration Demo) is an optical imaging payload launching on a 12U CubeSat in June 2026 as the first technology demonstration for the CuRIOS constellation concept. The payload uses commercial components, including an Atik apx60 camera with a Sony IMX455 detector. CuRIOS-ED was fully integrated into the spacecraft in November 2025. In addition to camera-level characterization, we performed system-level thermal testing of the CuRIOS-ED payload to quantify thermal gradients and detector cooling behavior under flight-like conditions.    In this talk, we present the expected on-orbit performance of CuRIOS-ED based on these measurements, including predicted noise and thermal stability. Additionally, we outline the commissioning plan and expected science returnables. Early telemetry and images—if available—will be used to validate estimates and demonstrate the viability of low-cost CMOS imagers for future survey missions.

Items.Authors: Luca Zampieri, Michele Fiori, Alessia Spolon, Gabriele Rodeghiero, Luigi Lessio, Pietro Bruno, Carmelo Gargano, Giampiero Naletto, Giovanni Pareschi, Salvatore Scuderi, Gino Tosti
Items.Title: Integration of the Stellar Intensity Interferometry Instrument on the ASTRI Mini-Array
Items.Abstract: The ASTRI Mini-Array is an International collaboration, led by INAF, that is constructing and operating an array of nine Cherenkov Telescopes. The ASTRI Stellar Intensity Interferometry Instrument (SI3) is a fast single-photon-counting instrument for performing intensity interferometric observations of bright stars with the ASTRI Mini-Array. It is the first implementation of very narrow-band, multi-channel intensity interferometry in photon counting on Cherenkov telescopes with sub-nanosecond sampling. ASTRI SI3 will exploit the simultaneous 100-700 m baselines of the ASTRI Mini-Array to achieve angular resolutions below 100 microarcsec in the visible band and a dense coverage of the U-V plane. In Nov 2025 and Apr 2026 the first units were successfully integrated on the ASTRI telescopes in Tenerife. Here we present the activities carried out during these technical shifts and the plans for the full integration and commissioning of the instrument.

Items.Authors: Pierre Baudoz, Elsa Huby, Paulina Palma-Bifani, Olivier Dupuis, Fabrice Vidal, Nicolas Levraud, Yann Clénet, Joost A. van den Born, David Doelman, Ric Davies
Items.Title: The MICADO first light imager for the ELT: evaluating MICADO’s high contrast mode for direct imaging of exoplanets and disks
Items.Abstract: MICADO, the first-light near-infrared imager for the ELT, includes a dedicated high-contrast mode for observing exoplanets and circumstellar disks. It will offer better sensitivity and angular resolution than instruments like SPHERE and GPI, enabling major advances in studying planetary systems. MICADO features multiple high contrast tools, including Lyot coronagraphs, a vector-apodizing phase plate, and sparse aperture masks. Simulations show it will expand the parameter space for detecting young massive exoplanets at smaller separations and around more distant stars, creating strong synergies with GAIA and radial-velocity surveys. Its improved performance will also allow detection of fainter, more distant debris disks and finer imaging of nearby systems. A high-resolution (R = 20,000) long-slit spectroscopic mode will support detailed characterization of exoplanetary atmospheres. This work outlines MICADO’s development, expected performance, key science cases, and detection limits.

Items.Authors: Michael Bottom, Gustav M. Pettersson, Guillaume Huber, Robert A. Simcoe, Pavaman Bilgi, Charles-Antoine Claveau, Shane M. Jacobson
Items.Title: Fundamental noise limits of infrared detectors in the presence of readout glow
Items.Abstract: Read noise in infrared sensor arrays remains a major obstacle for ground- and space-based astronomy. Extremely large telescopes cannot reach their potential without major reductions in read noise, and it is a prohibitive constraint on the Habitable Worlds Observatory, which aims to detect and characterize nearby Earth-like exoplanets.    The standard approach of averaging multiple non-destructive reads typically yields only 2-3x improvement, far short of theoretical expectations, with 1/f noise often cited as the cause. Here we show that the poor averaging behavior is largely explained by readout glow: infrared emission from sensor electronics that injects electrons into pixels during readout. We derive the resulting sensitivity limits for both conventional and amplified sensors and present simulations and laboratory data demonstrating this effect across both architectures.

Items.Authors: Marshall W. Bautz, Eric D. Miller, Christopher Leitz, Gregory Prigozhin, Sven Hermann, Kevan Donlon, Beverly LaMarr, Tanmoy Chattopadhyay, Jill Juneau, Peter Orel, Keith Warner, Catherine Grant, Haley R. Stueber, Michael Cooper, Abigail Y. Pan, R. Glenn Morris, Steven W. Allen, Declan O'Neill
Items.Title: Detector technology development for a NASA probe mission concept: success through long-term collaboration
Items.Abstract: Future strategic X-ray observatories require much larger effective areas and significantly wider fields of view than their predecessors, while delivering comparable spatial and spectral resolution. Such missions require megapixel image sensors capable of frame-rates more than an order of magnitude faster than legacy devices with no loss of spectral resolution or passband. Our collaboration, comprising the MIT Kavli Institute, MIT Lincoln Laboratory and Stanford University, has worked toward this goal with NASA support for nearly a decade. We report successful demonstration of a prototype flight sensor for the Advanced X-ray Imaging Satellite (AXIS) mission concept. This 2-megapixel CCD can operate at 11 frames/second (twice the rate required for AXIS) with read noise as low as 3 electrons RMS. We present X-ray performance of this sensor and review its development history. We outline efforts to improve noise and readout speed beyond AXIS requirements for future X-ray observatories.

Items.Authors: Luis Alberto Rodriguez Garcia, Raul Dominguez Dominguez, Héctor de Paz Martín, Manuel Huertas López, Sebastian Fernandez Garcia, Francisco J. Rodríguez, Jorge de La Rosa, Camilo E. Jiménez, Romano Corradi, Axel Yanes, Fernando Rueda, Sergio Rueda, Antonio Marin-Franch, Javier Cenarro
Items.Title: Cognitive artificial intelligence ecosystem with intelligent agents for GTC operations
Items.Abstract: This work presents a cognitive AI ecosystem for the Gran Telescopio Canarias that combines edge-level deep learning with intelligent agents orchestrating actions across control, maintenance and administrative systems.     A three-layer architecture is introduced—cognitive, orchestration and operational—together with a phased roadmap towards operational, predictive and institutional intelligence. The contribution highlights governance principles and organizational requirements, and showcases practical use cases.     The approach aims to evolve the GTC into a cognitive observatory where the digital twin becomes an active, learning component that enhances resilience and reduces cognitive load for human teams.

Items.Authors: Stefan Kuiper, Matias Kidron, Kristian Boot, Arjo Bos, Bert Dekker, Jan Kuijt, Douwe Jan IJlst, Eugenoi Di Iorio, Jan de Vreugd, Max Baeten, Thijs Moens, Matthew Maniscalco, Wouter Jonker, Mark Chun, Ellen Lee, Suzanne Zhang, Alan Ryan, Luke McKay, Rachel Rampy, Christoph Baranec, Olivier Lai
Items.Title: Integration and acceptance testing of the UH2.2 adaptive secondary mirror
Items.Abstract: TNO is developing Adaptive Secondary Mirrors (ASM’s) based on inhouse developed Hybrid Variable Reluctance actuators. The high efficiency of these actuators allows for thicker mirror shells and eliminates the need for active cooling, resulting in high performance and reliability. In collaboration with the University of Hawaii, TNO developed two ASM prototypes: one for the NASA IRTF telescope (24 cm, 36 actuators), successfully tested in April 2024, and another for the UH-88 telescope (62 cm, 204 actuators), which passed factory acceptance testing end of 2025. A major integration challenge is bonding the flexible mirror shell to the actuator array while minimizing shape errors. A specialized bonding procedure enables shape adjustment during assembly, achieving an unpowered mirror shape error within 15% of the actuator range. Post-integration, actuator performance is verified with capacitive sensors. These methods and results inform future integration and testing of larger ASM systems.

Items.Authors: James E. Rhoads, Sangeeta Malhotra, The REX Team
Items.Title: The Reionization Explorer, REX
Items.Abstract: The Reionization Explorer, REX, is a mission concept to map the progress of cosmological reionization using the interaction of (redshifted) Lyman alpha light with intergalactic gas.   REX will use a wide-area near infrared camera with unique narrow-bandpass filters to identify the youngest, most actively star forming galaxies at cosmic dawn through Lyman alpha line emission.  Lyman alpha is the strongest emission line of hydrogen, and is resonantly scattered by neutral hydrogen. REX will map neutral and ionized intergalactic gas through the spatial distribution of Lyman alpha sources.    REX's baseline survey is 100 deg^2 in eight narrowband filters with central wavelengths from 0.97 to 1.46 microns, corresponding to redshifts 7-11 for Lyman alpha. This survey will have many other applications, including time domain astrophysics, galaxy evolution, interstellar medium studies, and outer solar system bodies. Still more is possible by using REX hardware for additional observations.

Items.Authors: Felix Meeker-Fuerst, Peter Kretschmar, Erik Kuulkers, Aitor Ibarra, Laura Tomás
Items.Title: XMM-Newton in the time-domain era
Items.Abstract: XMM-Newton’s large effective area and good time and spectral resolution in the X-ray band make it a cornerstone for time-domain astrophysics. Originally launched without provisions for target of opportunity (ToO) observations, the mission has evolved to deliver rapid responses to transient phenomena, with an increasing fraction of observing time used for these. In 2024, over 4 Ms, nearly one-third of annual science time, was dedicated to ToOs, frequently coordinated with other observatories, adding to the challenge of scheduling. This trend will intensify as multi-messenger and time-domain astronomy expand. To meet this challenge, the XMM-Newton SOC is implementing innovations such as automated observation sequence generation for specific science cases and rapid dissemination of quick-look data products. With these developments XMM-Newton will continue to support world-leading time-domain science and ensure excellent responsiveness well into the next decade.

Items.Authors: James Dunlop, Benoit Neichel, Stephen Chittick, Anne Costille, David Le Mignant, Calum Lithgow, Adriana de Lorenzo-Caceres, Mark Swinbank, William Taylor, Matthias Tecza, HARMONI CONSORTIUM
Items.Title: HARMONI at ELT: the revitalised high-resolution near-infrared IFU for the ESO ELT
Items.Abstract: HARMONI is the first light, adaptive optics assisted,  near-IR integral field spectrograph for the ELT. It covers a spectral range from 800nm to 2450nm with resolving powers from 3000 to 7000 and spatial sampling of 25mas and 6mas. It can operate in two adaptive optics modes - SCAO (including a high contrast capability) and MCAO.   This paper will present the current status of the project and highlight the enormous scientific potential of the renewed HARMONI behind the MCAO system (MORFEO) on the ELT. We will provide a high-level overview of the rescoped instrument design, its revolutionary capabilities, and anticipated performance. Finally, we will showcase representative examples of the transformative scientific breakthroughs that HARMONI will enable, through the detailed astrophysical study of the sources being uncovered by the new generation of multi-frequency surveys, ranging from potentially habitable exoplanets to the very first galaxies that reionized the Universe.

Items.Authors: Cristina-Maria Cordun, Harish Vedantham, Maaijke Mevius
Items.Title: Assessing ionospheric effects on image quality in the LOFAR Decametre Sky Survey
Items.Abstract: At decametre wavelengths, the ionosphere is a major barrier to high-resolution radio imaging. Its rapidly varying, direction-dependent phase errors can blur compact sources, reduce recovered flux densities, and cause strong field-to-field variations in image quality. We study these effects using three overlapping pointings from the LOFAR Decametre Sky Survey, observed under different ionospheric conditions. From phase-calibration solutions on a bright source, we measure the spatial diffractive scale, temporal decorrelation time, and angular scale over which calibration solutions remain transferable. These diagnostics are reflected in the final images. The field with the weakest ionospheric phase structure gives the sharpest compact sources and most reliable flux-density scale, while the strongest phase structure produces substantial source broadening and flux loss. This shows that spatial ionospheric structure is the dominant limitation.

Items.Authors: Konstantinos Vogiatzis, Rod Conan, Henry Fitzpatrick
Items.Title: Compensation for telescope thermal collimation errors using machine learning
Items.Abstract: This paper presents a strategy to connect the information provided by the Giant Magellan Telescope ambient and telescope structure temperature sensors to expected thermal deformation of the telescope structure at the interfaces with the primary and secondary mirrors and ultimately to optical corrective motions. This relationship between structure thermal deformations and optical misalignment is established through a digital database created by a neural network model with the goal of integrating into the wavefront control software. The database should be able to provide information on the required range of optical motions to maintain telescope collimation. The applicability and level of accuracy of the model are demonstrated using imposed (known) temperature fields.

Items.Authors: Michael W. Davis, Thomas K. Greathouse, Sue A. Ferrell, Maarten H. Versteeg, Kurt D. Retherford, Tracy M. Becker, Matthew A. Freeman, Rohini S. Giles, Erica R. Johnson, Philippa M. Molyneux, Aaliyah S. Richlen, Bradley J. Trantham
Items.Title: Deep space operation of a curved borosilicate glass microchannel plate detector: results from the Europa Clipper ultraviolet spectrograph in-flight commissioning and early calibration
Items.Abstract: We present the results of the Europa Clipper ultraviolet spectrograph (Europa-UVS) commissioning and early in-flight calibration. Commissioning activities included measurements of detector dark noise and optimizing detector HV level via observations of the interplanetary Lyman-alpha. Dark rates matched those measured on the ground. HV levels were nominal for the operational temperature. Observations with the high-spatial resolution aperture confirmed the sharpened focus when compared to nominal observations. Later calibration activities included a raster scan of a star along the UVS slit. These observations confirmed the UVS pointing with respect to the nominal spacecraft nadir-pointing, as well as UVS sensitivity at wavelengths beyond 110 nm. UVS in-flight sensitivity matched ground calibration measurements, confirming that there was no degradation of UVS sensitivity in the three years between ground calibration measurements and in-flight calibration.

Items.Title: Status of BICEP array and integration of the 220/270 GHz receiver
Items.Abstract: BICEP Array (BA), the latest in the BICEP/Keck series of experiments, is a set of small-aperture microwave telescopes designed to detect faint polarization signals in the cosmic microwave background. BA will utilize highly sensitive receivers, tight systematic control, and a partnership with the South Pole Telescope for delensing to constrain the amplitude of inflationary polarization.  Two BA telescopes, one observing at 30 and 40 GHz and the other at 150 GHz, have been collecting data for multiple years. The most recently deployed telescope in the array, which observes at 220/270 GHz, was deployed in the 2024-25 austral summer. This higher-frequency telescope provides unprecedented constraining power for the galactic dust foreground.

Items.Authors: Jenny Atwood, Mohammad Islam
Items.Title: Adaptive secondary mirrors: a survey of current systems, emerging technologies, and future directions
Items.Abstract: Adaptive Secondary Mirrors (ASMs) are critical elements of advanced Adaptive Optics (AO) systems, enabling high-speed wavefront correction at the telescope secondary. This paper surveys ASM technology from operational systems at LBT and VLT to new designs for GMT and ELT. Membrane materials are reviewed for stiffness, thermal stability, and manufacturability, including testing challenges for concave and convex geometries. Actuator technologies—electromagnetic, piezoelectric, and hybrid systems—are compared for performance and scalability. The paper concludes with future directions, highlighting NRC Herzberg’s exploration of composite mirrors as candidate technology for next-generation ASMs.

Items.Authors: Yi Hu, Junhui Shi, Jia Ma, Zhenyao Yang, Zhongyue Chen, Zhongna Dong, Yiming Liang, Jiacheng Zhang, Zhichao Zheng, Yuqi Wang, Yongxiong Xiao, Haoyuan Du, Xu Yang, Zhaohui Shang, Yongna Mao, Jifeng Liu
Items.Title: Embodied artificial intelligence telescope: an effective solution for high-level autonomous operation requirements of GOTTA project
Items.Abstract: Future time-domain astronomy will rely on globally distributed arrays of wide-field telescopes capable of tracking the most rapid and violent cosmic phenomena in real time. This facility can only operate effectively if it is fully autonomous, distributed, and continuously adaptive—capabilities that far exceed the limits of today’s open-loop robotic telescope software. We therefore introduce the Embodied Artificial Intelligence Telescope (EAIT), an AI-native closed-loop observational system that integrates perception, interpretation, planning, and action within each telescope. EAIT transforms a telescope from a passive data-collection instrument into an intelligent agent capable of real-time decision-making and autonomous coordination across a global array. Our results highlight the feasibility of EAIT and its potential to redefine the operational paradigm for next-generation transient astronomy.

Items.Title: LSST camera installation and commissioning
Items.Abstract: The world largest digital camera, LSST Camera, was delivered to the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in May 2024. From then began an extensive campaign integrating the camera into the Simonyi Survey Telescope and the broader Rubin Observatory. This talk will discuss the installation, Integration and commissioning of LSSTCam within the Rubin Observatory. These activities occurred in four main phases each to be described in detail. The result of this process was the camera integrated within the observatory mechanically, electrically, computationally and through software. Additionally, routine operations and maintenance are handed by on site staff. This talk will conclude with some lessons learned during these periods.

Items.Authors: Akio K. Inoue, Issei Yamamura, Toyoaki Suzuki, Takao Nakagawa, Hidehiro Kaneda, Takeshi Hashigaya, Fumihide Iwamuro, Yuma Sugahara, Shinki Oyabu, Kentaro Motohara, Yasuhiro Hirahara, Eiichi Egami, Yuichi Harikane, Hideko Nomura, Takashi Moriya, Takehiko Wada, Tadayuki Kodama, Masami Ouchi, Toru Yamada, Shin Watanabe
Items.Title: Progress of the concept study of GREX-PLUS: Galaxy Reionization EXplorer and PLanetary Universe Spectrometer
Items.Abstract: GREX-PLUS (Galaxy Reionization EXplorer and PLanetary Universe Spectrometer) is one of the two candidates of ISAS/JAXA's Strategic L-class mission for 2030s. The 1.0m, 50 K cryogenic telescope will have a wide-field camera (WFC) of 0.5 square degree field-of-view in the 2-8 micron wavelength band. An optional high resolution spectrometer (HRS) with a wavelength resolution of 30,000 in the 10-18 micron band is also under discussion. The WFC field-of-view is 200 times larger than that of the James Webb Space Telescope. Since the wavelength coverage of the similarly wide-field imaging telescopes of Euclid and Roman is limited to less than ~2 micron, the GREX-PLUS coverage of the wavelength longer than 2 micron is complementary and unique. The spectral resolution of the HRS is 10 times higher than that of the James Webb Space Telescope, opening a new window of the mid-infrared high resolution spectroscopy from space. I will present the latest status of the concept study of GREX-PLUS.

Items.Authors: Jamie A. Kennea
Items.Title: The Constant Operational Evolution of the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory
Items.Abstract: The Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, a pioneering time-domain and multi-messenger mission, predates the term “TDAMM.” Initially conceived to unravel the mystery of short Gamma Ray Bursts, Swift’s automated rapid response and multi-wavelength capabilities make it ideal for TDAMM research. Its continuous capability development, fostered by a highly motivated partnership between Flight and Science Operations teams, transformed Swift from a GRB detection and follow-up mission to a TOO machine, averaging 6 TOOs daily and capable of automated response within seconds. Swift also boasts unique capabilities in Gravitational Wave follow-up, including deep sensitive detection of prompt emission, large-scale tiling of probable counterpart galaxies, and the possibility of repointing before the merger to catch the emission “on the fly”.

Items.Authors: Alessandro Marconi, Paolo Di Marcantonio, Alessio Zanutta, Roberto Maiolino, Livia Origlia, Marco Landoni, Ernesto Oliva, Marco Riva, on behalf of ANDES Consortium
Items.Title: ANDES, the high-resolution spectrograph for the ELT: science drivers, instrument overview, and project status
Items.Abstract: ANDES is the high-resolution optical/NIR spectrograph for the ELT, simultaneously covering 0.40–1.8 μm (goal: 0.35–2.4 μm) at R≈100,000. Its fiber-fed, modular design provides high stability, wide coverage, and multiple modes, including seeing-limited spectroscopy, a SCAO-assisted NIR IFU, a high-dispersion coronagraph, and a faint-target mode. ANDES will enable major advances in exoplanet atmospheres, the first stars, fundamental physics, and cosmic acceleration. Developed by a consortium of 30+ institutes in 13 countries, the project has completed the System Architecture Review and is advancing toward the Preliminary Design Review in mid-2026, including work on the U- and K-band extensions.

Items.Authors: Martin de Wit, Kenichiro Nagayoshi, Luciano Gottardi, Emanuele Taralli, Sven Visser, Kevin Ravensberg, Jian-Rong Gao, Jan-Willem A. den Herder
Items.Title: Characterization of a large-format x-ray microcalorimeter array based on transition edge sensors
Items.Abstract: We report on the development and cryogenic tests of a full-sized array of Transition Edge Sensors (TESs)  designed for the X-ray Integral Field Unit (X-IFU). The wafer, comprising a fully-wired array of over 1500  high-performance TES microcalorimeters, was fabricated to meet the stringent requirements of the X-IFU. The  quality of the full-sized array is assessed by the study of representative smaller arrays on pop-out diagnostic chips  located near the mean array on the same wafer. Characterization is performed using a dedicated DC-biased  setup featuring PTB SQUIDs and SRON lithographically-defined shunt resistors and Nyquist inductors. Comprehensive measurements at milliKelvin temperatures were conducted to evaluate the detector uniformity, transition parameters, noise characteristics, and energy resolution. Our results demonstrate excellent uniformity over all devices tested on  the different diagnostic chips, and show the readiness of our technology for future X-ray observatories.

Items.Authors: Daniele Vassallo, Dino Mesa, Guido Agapito, Fabio Rossi, Alfio Puglisi
Items.Title: Enhancing SHARK-NIR detection capabilities through differentiable PSF rendering
Items.Abstract: We present a novel post-processing method for SHARK-NIR at the LBT, based on a differentiable coronagraphic PSF model. Our technique combines a physics-based forward model of the instrument optics with adaptive optics (AO) residual wavefront information to refine the instantaneous stellar PSF via gradient-based optimization directly from science images. This approach enables data-driven correction of quasi-static aberrations and speckle variability, overcoming the limitations of traditional post-processing techniques. We validate the method using realistic numerical simulations of SHARK-NIR observations and present preliminary results on real on-sky data. The technique enhances SHARK-NIR’s capability to detect faint companions and paves the way for PSF-aware analysis pipelines for current and future high-contrast imaging instruments.

Items.Authors: Bryan J. Butler, Rick Perley, Tony Willis, Evangelia Tremou, Eric Greisen, Benjamin Hugo
Items.Title: Faraday rotation correction for polarization calibration of low frequency observations
Items.Abstract: Imaging polarimetry at meter wavelengths requires removal of the variable ionospheric Faraday rotation (IFRM) with an accuracy of 0.1 rad/m^2 or better. Methods to estimate the IFRM using GNSS timing data have been developed. Evaluating the accuracy of these estimates requires observations of a source of known intrinsic electric vector position angle (EVPA) over a wide rage of ionospheric conditions. At meter wavelengths, the Moon is the only source of a priori known polarized emission which can be used for this.    Using VLA and MeerKAT observations, we have tested the accuracy of seven IFRM estimates generated using data from global VTEC maps. Additionally, we have tested the IFRM estimates derived using GNSS data from nearby stations directly. The estimates based on global maps consistently overestimate the magnitude of the IFRM by 0.3 to 1.0 rad/m^2, whereas the estimates using local GNSS data are within 0.1 rad/m^2 of those derived from the lunar data.

Items.Authors: Marie Laslandes, Stefan Ströbele, Lucas Munoz, Aline Pham, Pierre-Yves Madec, Julien Charton
Items.Title: High stability deformable mirror with large number of actuators for astronomical telescopes: requirements and performance
Items.Abstract: The next generation of instruments for very and extremely large telescopes is requiring adaptive optics systems more and more efficient in correcting atmospheric turbulence. For most instruments, this is translating into larger number of actuators and faster deformable mirrors (DM). There is also an increasing need for better stability of the DM surface when its shape is not controlled.   In this paper, we present the requirements, the development and the performance of a 93 mm diameter DM with 3228 actuators with improved mirror performance without need for closed loop control. This DM type was developed by Bertin Alpao in collaboration with ESO and will be used in the MAVIS instrument.

Items.Authors: Juan Carlos Guerra, Sam Ragland
Items.Title: Machine learning approaches to improve telescope efficiency and AO instrument strategies
Items.Abstract: Efficient LBT operation requires each acquisition to start near the correct pointing and active-secondary collimation state. We present a telemetry-driven Random Forest/Quantile Regression Forest framework to predict residual CA/IE pointing terms and ASM hexapod coordinates for LUCI and LBTI. The models use azimuth, elevation, thermal telemetry, time of night, instrument, side, and collimation history within the operations window. We separate true cold-start predictions, using only pre-acquisition telemetry, from short-horizon updates that use recent same-instrument measurements. A strict 2026-06-16 HD116405 leave-one-day-out test compares pure CA/IE cold start, hexapod bootstrap, chained CA/IE using predicted hexapod state, and diagnostic CA/IE using measured hexapod state. The framework provides uncertainty-aware recommendations to reduce acquisition overhead and long-tail correction events without replacing the operator or analytical pointing model
